newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African mercenaries expelled from PNG return home.
newsitem.headline: S.African mercenaries expelled from PNG return home.

text.p: South African mercenaries hired by Papua New Guinea to put down an island rebellion arived home on Saturday, expelled by the soldiers they were meant to have helped.
Arriving on a flight from Hong Kong carrying little or no luggage, the South Africans, most of them black, tensely declined all comment on their stint in the South Pacific.

Two white mercenaries, shielding their faces with cardboard packages, swore on seeing waiting journalists and threatened to hit a cameraman filming them before turning their backs to the cameras and stalking off.
A pilot on the flight told Reuters he had 48 men on board from Papua New Guinea.
"They wanted to go home. As far as they are concerned the adventure is over for them," said Major Walter Enuma, the soldier in charge of expelling the mercenaries from Papua New Guinea
"They weren't really deported, we thought it was safer to bring them out," a woman coordinating the group's arrival told reporters.

Confirming she was from Executive Outcomes, the Pretoria- based group which hires out former South African Defence Force soldiers to foreign governments, the woman apologised for the two men's aggressive behaviour.
"They are very professional. They didn't look so good when they came in because they're tired from the flight and I think the stress of the last few days...," she commented.
The woman, who did not give her name, said the men should not be seen as mercenaries, adding: "We don't like them to be called that -- they are consultants."
The group left Papua New Guinea on Friday but troops handed their commander, former British colonel Tim Spicer over to police.
A police spokesman said Spicer, a former top U.N. peacekeeper in Bosnia who also served in the Falkands and Gulf wars, would be questioned and could then be released.
British diplomats in Port Moresby were waiting for him to be handed over to them.

Spicer heads the British firm Sandline International which signed a $36 million dollar contract to provide Papua New Guinea with commandos and hardware to crush a nine-year-old revolt in Bougainville.
The plan backfired on Monday when army commander Brigadier- General Jerry Singirok turned on Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan, demanding that he quit and terminate the mercenary contract.
